meta.summary: The needs, wants, and interests that propel organisms in certain directions — what makes us do what we do; what drives our actions.

sections.title: Biological Basis of Motivation to Eat

blocks.name: Motives
blocks.def: The needs, wants, and interests that propel organisms in certain directions — what makes us do what we do; what drives our actions.

blocks.name: Motivation
blocks.def: The force/energy that initiates, guides, and maintains goal-oriented behaviours. It causes us to take action — whether grabbing a snack to reduce hunger, or enrolling in college to earn a degree. The forces underlying motivation can be biological, social, emotional, or cognitive.

sections.title: Biological Basis of Motivation to Eat

blocks.x: Hunger is the sensation felt when one has a physiological need to eat; satiety is the absence of hunger — feeling full. Hunger is influenced by the brain, blood sugar/digestive factors, and hormones.

blocks.name: Brain regulation
blocks.def: Most biological hunger originates in the hypothalamus. The lateral hypothalamus (LH), when stimulated, causes hunger; if damaged, a person never feels hungry again and may lose weight. The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is the satiety center — stimulation makes you feel full; damage means never feeling full, causing weight gain. The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is also involved in hunger regulation.

blocks.name: Glucose & digestive regulation
blocks.def: Glucose is a simple sugar and key energy source. Activities that decrease blood sugar increase hunger; activities that increase blood sugar promote fullness. Glucostats — neurons sensitive to glucose — monitor blood glucose fluctuations in the brain. After eating, the vagus nerve carries information about stomach stretching, signalling fullness.

blocks.name: Hormonal regulation
blocks.def: Leptin (made by fat cells) decreases appetite and signals the brain about sufficient energy stores — but many obese people don't respond to leptin's signals despite higher levels. Ghrelin (released mainly in the stomach) increases appetite and signals hunger — it rises before eating and falls for about three hours afterward. Ghrelin levels rise in children with anorexia nervosa and fall in children who are obese.

blocks.name: <term d="Doing something because it is satisfying in itself, not for an outside reward.">Intrinsic motivation</term>
blocks.def: Performing an activity for the pleasure or value of the activity itself, not for an external goal (e.g. playing games, reading, listening to music). Considered the only path to sustainable, long-term motivation — though some extrinsic factors can become internalized, typically requiring at least some intrinsic factors too. Driven by four factors: Autonomy (control over one's life/activities), Mastery (getting better at what you do), Relatedness (feeling connected to others), and Purpose (being part of something greater).

blocks.name: <term d="Doing something to gain an outside reward or to avoid a punishment.">Extrinsic motivation</term>
blocks.def: Performing an activity toward an external goal — doing something because of what you'll get, or to avoid something undesired (e.g. working for money, studying hard for an 'A', avoiding being scolded).

blocks.name: Biological motives
blocks.def: Originate in bodily needs — hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep, rest. Reflect needs essential to survival; people share the same biological motives, though social motives depend on individual experience.

blocks.name: Social motives
blocks.def: Originate from social experiences — achievement, affiliation, autonomy, dominance, order. People can acquire an unlimited number of social needs through <term d="A relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience.">learning</term> and socializing (unlike the limited number of biological needs); some social motives fuel intrinsic motivation. Strength varies from person to person.

blocks.x: Each theory is limited in scope on its own, but together they build a fuller understanding of motivation. Six major theories: <term d="An internal state of tension created by a need, which pushes a person to act to reduce it.">Drive</term>, <term d="An external goal or reward that pulls a person toward acting in a certain way.">Incentive</term>, Behaviorist, Humanistic, <term d="The level of alertness and physiological activation a person is experiencing.">Arousal</term>, and Evolutionary theory.

blocks.name: Drive theory
blocks.def: A drive is an internal state of tension motivating an organism to act to reduce that tension (e.g. hunger). Based on homeostasis — physiological equilibrium. Explains behaviours with a strong biological component well (e.g. eating reduces the hunger drive). Limitation: can't explain motivation without drive arousal — e.g. eating dessert after already being full.

blocks.name: Incentive theory
blocks.def: An incentive is an external reward/goal with the capacity to motivate behaviour (e.g. a promotion, an 'A', money, praise). People are pulled toward positive incentives and pushed away from negative ones. Emphasizes environmental factors, downplaying biological motivation. Applications: bonuses, praise, opportunities, promotions, salary increases, paid time off.

blocks.x: Drive vs. Incentive: drive theories say internal tension pushes behaviour (source is within the organism); incentive theories say external stimuli pull behaviour (source is outside the organism).

blocks.name: Behaviorist theory
blocks.def: Emphasizes the environment as key, especially extrinsic contributions. Grounded in operant conditioning — rewards and punishments shape future behaviour.

blocks.name: Humanistic theory
blocks.def: Maslow proposed motivation relies on a hierarchy of needs — basic deficiency needs at the bottom, advanced growth needs above, topped by self-actualization (fulfilling true potential). Each level must be satisfied before the next can be pursued. Self-actualization is the ultimate human motivator.

blocks.name: Arousal theory
blocks.def: People are driven to maintain an optimum level of physiological arousal. When arousal drops too low (boredom), people seek stimulation; when too high (overstimulation), people seek relaxing activities. Individual differences exist in what's 'optimal' — some seek thrills (car racing, sky diving), others prefer calm activities (reading).

blocks.name: Yerkes-Dodson Law
blocks.def: Performance increases with arousal up to an optimal point, then decreases with further arousal increase. E.g. students perform best with moderate exam <term d="A state of apprehension and heightened arousal about a possible threat.">anxiety</term> — too little makes them inattentive, too much interferes with thinking.

blocks.name: Evolutionary (instinctual) theory
blocks.def: Natural selection favours behaviours/motives that maximize reproductive success. These are believed to be instinctual fixed action patterns — stereotypical behaviours performed automatically the same way by all members of a species in response to a specific stimulus. Examples: aggression, dominance, attraction, affiliation, achievement, curiosity. E.g. dominance is more prominent in males, providing reproductive/survival advantages in many species.

items: Business: commission pay tying compensation to performance objectives; generous bonuses for top performers; intangible rewards alongside monetary compensation.
Classroom: use of cognitive theory — praise/reward as a strategy to motivate performance (e.g. awards at ceremonies motivating others to aspire).
Health care: understanding what motivates health-related behaviours (e.g. smoking cessation, dietary change, exercise adherence) to design more effective interventions.

mnemonics.h: SLC — three cues for abnormal behaviour
lines: Statistical infrequency, personal distress, and maladaptive/impaired functioning — the three go-to criteria for spotting abnormal behaviour.

mnemonics.h: HOMER — <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it more likely to happen again.">reinforcement</term> vs <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it less likely to happen again.">punishment</term>
lines: Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it — regardless of whether something is added (positive) or removed (negative).

mnemonics.h: ABC of <term d="The view that psychology should study only observable behaviour, not private mental states.">behaviourism</term>
lines: Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence — the basic chain behaviourists analyse to explain why a behaviour keeps happening.

mnemonics.h: DEPC — the four goals of <term d="The scientific study of behaviour and of the mental processes behind it.">psychology</term>
lines: Describe, Explain/understand, Predict, Control — the four things every psychological study is ultimately trying to do.

mnemonics.h: PIE — Freud's structure of <term d="The characteristic pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving that makes a person distinctive.">personality</term>
lines: <term d="In Freudian theory, the primitive part of the mind demanding immediate gratification.">id</term> (Pleasure), <term d="In Freudian theory, the part of the mind that balances demands against reality.">ego</term> (reality — 'I'), <term d="In Freudian theory, the internalised moral standards of society.">superego</term> (morality — think '<term d="The moral principles governing how research and practice should be conducted.">Ethics</term>') — the three parts constantly negotiating behaviour.
Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules (like gambling) are the hardest to extinguish — Very Resistant to stopping.
